tool.name: PowerShell
tool.tagline: Cross-platform object-based shell and scripting language from Microsoft
tool.description: PowerShell is a shell and scripting language built on .NET in which commands (cmdlets) pass structured objects through the pipeline instead of text. It is the standard automation tool for Windows, Active Directory, Microsoft 365 and Azure, and PowerShell 7 runs on Windows, Linux and macOS. Learning it lets you script system administration and cloud tasks with real data types, error handling and modules.

glossary.def: A built-in PowerShell command with a Verb-Noun name, such as Get-Process or Remove-Item.
PowerShell's naming pattern for commands: an approved verb, a dash, then a noun, as in Get-Process or New-Item.
In PowerShell, a short nickname for a command, such as gci for Get-ChildItem.
Microsoft's platform and large library of ready-made code that PowerShell is built on; PowerShell's objects are .NET objects.
PowerShell's shortcut where asking a list of objects for a property returns that property from each item, as in (Get-Process).Name.
A piece of PowerShell code in curly braces { } that can be handed to a command and run later, often once per object.
A column you add to Select-Object output, written @{ Name = '...'; Expression = { ... } }, computed from each object.
In PowerShell, $( ) inside double-quoted text: the code inside runs and its result is inserted, as in "Files: $($files.Count)".
A variable PowerShell fills in for you, such as $PSVersionTable, $PID, $HOME, $_ or $true.
In PowerShell, an adapter that shows a data store (files, environment variables, Windows settings, certificates) as a drive the same cmdlets can browse.
PowerShell's lookup table of key = value pairs, written @{ Name = 'Ada'; Role = 'admin' }.
Passing a hashtable (or array) of parameters to a command with @ instead of $, as in Get-ChildItem @params.
PowerShell's standard simple object, created with [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'web1'; CPU = 72 }: properties in the order you give them.
Parameters every cmdlet and advanced function accepts automatically, such as -Verbose, -ErrorAction and -WhatIf.
A PowerShell function marked [CmdletBinding()] that behaves like a cmdlet: common parameters, pipeline input and more.
A PowerShell error that stops the current statement and can be caught with try/catch, such as one from throw or -ErrorAction Stop.
A PowerShell error that is reported but lets the command carry on with the next item; try/catch doesn't see it.
The object PowerShell creates for an error, holding the exception, the object involved and where it happened; $_ inside catch.
A Windows-only PowerShell setting that controls whether scripts may run; a safety net against accidents, not a security barrier.
Running a script with a dot and a space (. ./file.ps1) so its functions and variables stay available afterwards.
A script PowerShell runs at every start, at the path stored in $PROFILE; a place for your own aliases and functions.
The public website where PowerShell modules are published and installed from.
The PowerShell 7.4+ cmdlets (Find-PSResource, Install-PSResource) that search for and install modules from the PowerShell Gallery.
A .psd1 file describing a PowerShell module: its version, author, dependencies and which functions it makes public.
An isolated place where PowerShell runs code, with its own variables; parallel loops and thread jobs each get one.
A PowerShell background task started with Start-ThreadJob that runs on another thread inside the same process.
Running PowerShell commands on other computers, over WinRM (Windows) or SSH.
Windows Remote Management: Windows' built-in service PowerShell remoting uses to run commands on other Windows computers.
PowerShell sending a collection down the pipeline one item at a time, so a one-item array arrives as just that item.
A prefix such as $script:, $global: or $using: that says which scope a variable belongs to.
The standard testing framework for PowerShell code.

concepts.name: Cmdlets, Get-Help and Get-Command
concepts.summary: What PowerShell is, how its commands (cmdlets) are named, and how to find commands and read their help.
concepts.why: Finding commands yourself is the core PowerShell skill; everything else can be looked up.
concepts.body:
PowerShell is a **shell**: a program where you type commands to control your computer, running inside a **terminal**, the text window where commands go. It is also a scripting language, so the same commands can be saved in a file, a **script**, and run again later. Microsoft makes it, and PowerShell 7 runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

PowerShell's own commands are called **cmdlets** (say "command-lets"). Their names follow a **Verb-Noun** pattern: `Get-Process` lists running programs, `Set-Location` changes the current folder, `New-Item` creates a file or folder, and `Remove-Item` deletes one. The verbs come from a fixed list of approved verbs (`Get-Verb`), so once you know a noun you can often guess the command.

Extra words after a command change what it does. Each **parameter** starts with a dash and usually takes a value: `Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd'` shows today's date in that layout.

Names of commands and parameters are **case-insensitive**: capital letters don't matter, so `get-date` works too. A parameter name can also be shortened as long as it stays unambiguous: `-f` for `-Format`.

Three commands help you find your way:

- `Get-Command` searches for commands: `Get-Command -Noun *Service*` or `Get-Command *json*` (`*` stands for any characters).
- `Get-Help Name -Examples` shows usage examples, and `-Full` shows every parameter. Run `Update-Help` once to download the full help files, or use `-Online` to open the web page.
- `Get-Member` (next lesson) shows what a command's results contain.

Many cmdlets also have a short **alias**, a nickname: `gci` for `Get-ChildItem` (list files), `cd` for `Set-Location`, `%` for `ForEach-Object`. Aliases save typing when you work interactively, but write full names in saved scripts so others can read them. On Linux and macOS, names like `ls` and `cat` are not aliases: they run the system's own programs, which behave differently.

Two editions exist: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (`powershell.exe`, built into Windows and no longer developed) and PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`, **cross-platform**: it runs on all three systems). This course uses PowerShell 7.5; `$PSVersionTable` shows which one you have.
concepts.code:
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion.ToString()   # 7.5.3
Get-Command -Noun Process              # Get-Process, Start-Process, Stop-Process, ...
Get-Command *json* -CommandType Cmdlet # ConvertFrom-Json, ConvertTo-Json, Test-Json
Get-Alias gci                          # gci -> Get-ChildItem
Get-Help Get-ChildItem -Examples       # usage examples (run Update-Help once)
Get-Date -Format 'yyyy-MM-dd'          # 2026-10-17
get-date -f yyyy                       # case-insensitive, -f is short for -Format
(Get-Verb).Count                       # number of approved verbs
takeaways: Cmdlets are named Verb-Noun, and capitals don't matter
Get-Command finds commands; Get-Help -Examples shows how to use them
Aliases when typing, full names in scripts
pitfalls: Using aliases like ls or cat in scripts meant for every system: on Linux they run different programs with different output.

quiz.q: You need a cmdlet that stops a Windows service (a program running in the background) but don't know its name. What is the best first step?
quiz.explain: Get-Command -Noun Service lists Get-, Start-, Stop-, Restart-Service and the rest.

quiz.q: Which program is PowerShell 7?
quiz.explain: PowerShell 7 is pwsh; powershell.exe is the older Windows PowerShell 5.1.

concepts.name: Objects in the pipeline
concepts.summary: PowerShell passes objects with properties and methods from command to command, not text; Get-Member shows what they contain.
concepts.why: Thinking in objects instead of lines of text is what makes PowerShell different from other shells.
concepts.body:
Most older shells pass text from one command to the next, and you have to cut that text apart to find what you need. PowerShell passes **objects** instead: bundles of named data. A file object knows its name, size and date; a **process** object (one running program) knows its name and ID.

The **pipe** symbol `|` sends one command's results into the next command. A chain of commands joined this way is a **pipeline**: `Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object Length` lists files and sorts them by size. The objects travel through it intact; what you finally see on screen is just a formatted view made at the very end.

PowerShell is built on **.NET**, Microsoft's large collection of ready-made code, so its objects are .NET objects. `Get-Process` produces `Process` objects, and `Get-ChildItem` produces `FileInfo` and `DirectoryInfo` objects.

Because results are objects, you can:

- read their **properties**, the named pieces of data: `(Get-Date).Year`, `(Get-Item notes.txt).Length`;
- call their **methods**, actions they know how to do, with a dot and parentheses: `'text'.ToUpper()`, `(Get-Date).AddDays(7)`;
- sort, filter and pick by property name, without cutting up any text.

`Get-Member` (alias `gm`) shows what an object offers: pipe anything into it to see its type name, properties and methods. Objects usually have more properties than the default table shows; `Select-Object *` reveals them all.

Parentheses run a command first so you can use its result as a value: `(Get-ChildItem).Count`. Asking a whole list of objects for one property gives you that property from each of them (**member enumeration**), so `(Get-Process).Name` returns every process name.

Ordinary programs such as `git` or `ping` still produce text. Each line of their output becomes a **string** object (a piece of text) in the pipeline.
concepts.code:
$p = Get-Process -Id $PID       # $PID always holds the ID number of this PowerShell; $p is its process object
$p.GetType().FullName           # System.Diagnostics.Process   (the object's type name)
$p.ProcessName                  # pwsh
$p | Get-Member -MemberType Method | Select-Object -First 2 Name
                                # list only its methods, and show the first 2 names
Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File |   # $PSHOME holds the folder PowerShell is installed in
  Sort-Object Length -Descending |                # biggest files first
  Select-Object -First 3 Name, Length             # properties, not text columns
(Get-Date).AddDays(7).DayOfWeek # e.g. Saturday
'hello'.ToUpper()               # HELLO
(1..5 | Measure-Object -Sum).Sum  # 1..5 makes the numbers 1 to 5; Measure-Object -Sum adds them up: 15
(Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File).Name  # member enumeration: the Name of every file in that folder
takeaways: The pipeline passes objects, not text
Pipe to Get-Member to see properties and methods
(command).Property uses a command's result as a value
pitfalls: Cutting apart the text of the on-screen table instead of reading the objects' properties.

quiz.q: What travels between `Get-ChildItem | Sort-Object Length`?
quiz.explain: Cmdlets pass .NET objects; Sort-Object reads their Length property directly.

quiz.q: Which command shows the properties and methods of an object?
quiz.explain: Get-Member lists the type, properties and methods of whatever is piped into it.

concepts.name: Variables, types and strings
concepts.summary: Store values in $variables, know their types and conversions, and put values into text with double quotes.
concepts.why: Variables and text with values inserted appear on nearly every line of a PowerShell script.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name that holds a value, like a labelled jar. In PowerShell variable names start with `$`, and a variable is created the moment you store something in it: `$name = 'Ada'`. Spaces around `=` are fine, and names are case-insensitive.

Every value has a type (its **data type**), taken from .NET, which decides what you can do with it:

- `3` is an `Int32`, an **integer** (whole number).
- `3.5` is a `Double`, a **floating-point number** (one with a decimal point).
- `'x'` is a `String`, a piece of text, called a **string**.
- `$true` and `$false` are `Boolean` values, **booleans**: yes or no.
- `$null` means nothing at all (**null**).

Text comes in two flavours. **Double quotes** insert variables' values: `"Hello $name"` becomes `Hello Ada`. This is **string interpolation**. For anything more than a plain variable, such as a property or a calculation, use a **subexpression** `$( )`: `"Files: $($files.Count)"`. **Single quotes** keep text exactly as typed: `'Cost: $5'`.

Special characters inside text use the backtick `` ` `` (top-left key on most keyboards): `` `n `` is a new line and `` `t `` a tab. These codes are **escape sequences**. The backslash `\` is just a normal character, convenient for Windows file paths.

PowerShell converts types automatically (**type conversion**), and the value on the left decides how: `'42' + 1` gives the text `421`, while `1 + '42'` gives the number `43`. Convert on purpose by putting a type in square brackets in front: `[int]'42'` is the number 42. Writing `[int]$age = '30'` also locks the variable, so every later value must convert to a whole number.

Settings the system passes to every program, **environment variables**, live under `env:`: `$env:PATH` (the folders searched for programs) or `$env:HOME`. PowerShell also fills in **automatic variables** for you, such as `$PSVersionTable`, `$PID` (the ID of this running PowerShell), `$HOME`, `$true`, `$false` and `$null`.

When comparing with `$null`, put it on the left: `$null -eq $x` (`-eq` means "equals"; the next lesson explains why the order matters).
concepts.code:
$name = 'Ada'
$count = 3
"Hello $name, you have $count new messages"   # expands variables
'Hello $name'                     # Hello $name  (single quotes: literal)
"Total: $($count * 2)"            # Total: 6     ($() for expressions)
"Tab:`tdone"                      # Tab:    done (backtick escapes)
$count.GetType().Name             # Int32
'42' + 1                          # 421  (left operand is a string)
1 + '42'                          # 43
[int]'42' + 1                     # 43
[int]$age = '30'                  # constrained to int
$age.GetType().Name               # Int32
# $age = 'thirty'                 # error: cannot convert value "thirty" to type "System.Int32"
$null -eq $undefinedVariable      # True
$env:HOME                         # /home/you  (environment variable)
takeaways: Double quotes insert $var and $(expression); single quotes keep text as typed
The left value's type decides conversion: '42' + 1 is '421'
The backtick starts escape codes; $env:NAME reads environment variables
pitfalls: Writing "Size: $file.Length" and getting the whole object followed by '.Length'; use $($file.Length).

quiz.q: What does `'5' + 5` return?
quiz.explain: The left operand is a string, so + concatenates and 5 is converted to '5'.

quiz.q: With $f = Get-Item ./a.txt, which string shows the file size correctly?
quiz.explain: Only a subexpression inside double quotes evaluates the property access.

concepts.name: Filter, sort and select
concepts.summary: Shape a pipeline's results with Where-Object, Sort-Object, Select-Object, Group-Object and Measure-Object.
concepts.why: These five cmdlets answer most 'which ones, how many, the biggest' questions about any data.
concepts.body:
Once data is objects, five cmdlets answer most "which ones, how many, the biggest" questions:

- **Where-Object** filters: `Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB }` keeps files bigger than 1 MB (`-gt` means "greater than"). The code in curly braces is a **script block**, a piece of code handed to the cmdlet and run once per object, with `$_` (also called `$PSItem`) holding the current object. For one comparison, the shorter form `Where-Object Length -gt 1MB` works too.
- **Sort-Object** orders by one or more properties: `Sort-Object Length -Descending`.
- **Select-Object** picks properties (`Select-Object Name, Length`), takes the `-First` or `-Last` few items, drops repeats with `-Unique`, and `-ExpandProperty Name` gives the bare values instead of objects with one property.
- **Group-Object** puts objects with the same property value together and counts them.
- **Measure-Object** computes the count, sum, average, smallest and largest value.

A **calculated property** adds a new column computed from each object: `@{ Name = 'KB'; Expression = { $_.Length / 1KB } }`, a small table pairing a name with a script block. The size suffixes `KB`, `MB` and `GB` are built in: `1KB` is 1024.

**Filter left**: when a cmdlet has its own filter parameter, such as `Get-ChildItem -Filter *.log` or `Get-Process -Name pwsh`, use it. The command then skips unwanted items at the source, before objects are even created, which can be far faster than `Where-Object` on large sets, especially on other computers over the network.
concepts.code:
$files = Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File
$files | Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB } | Measure-Object |
  Select-Object -ExpandProperty Count            # how many files > 1 MB
$files | Where-Object Extension -eq '.json' |
  Select-Object -First 2 -ExpandProperty Name    # simplified syntax
$files | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 3 Name,
  @{ Name = 'KB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.Length / 1KB) } }
$files | Group-Object Extension | Sort-Object Count -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 3 Count, Name             # most common extensions
$files | Measure-Object Length -Sum -Maximum | Select-Object Count, Sum, Maximum
Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -Filter *.json             # filter left: provider does it
takeaways: Where-Object filters, Sort-Object orders, Select-Object picks
$_ is the current object inside a script block
Use a cmdlet's own -Filter or -Name parameter before Where-Object
pitfalls: Expecting `Select-Object Name` to return strings; it returns objects with a Name property. Use -ExpandProperty.

quiz.q: Which command returns plain strings of process names?
quiz.explain: -ExpandProperty unwraps the property value; plain Select-Object keeps objects with one property.

quiz.q: Why prefer `Get-ChildItem -Filter *.log` over piping to `Where-Object Name -like '*.log'`?
options: It filters before objects are created, so it is faster
quiz.explain: Filtering at the source avoids building and piping objects you would throw away.

concepts.name: Files, paths and providers
concepts.summary: Move around folders, read, write, copy and delete files, build file paths safely, and reach other data stores as drives.
concepts.why: Most automation reads or writes files, and the same cmdlets also reach settings and other data stores.
concepts.body:
Files live in folders, also called **directories**. A **file path** is a file's address: the folders you pass through to reach it, like `C:\Users\ada\notes.txt` on Windows or `/home/ada/notes.txt` on Linux and macOS.

A small, consistent set of cmdlets handles files: `Get-ChildItem` (list), `Set-Location` (move to a folder, alias `cd`), `New-Item`, `Copy-Item`, `Move-Item`, `Rename-Item`, `Remove-Item` and `Test-Path` (does it exist?). Their `-Path` parameter accepts wildcards (`*` matches any characters); use `-LiteralPath` for names that contain `[` or `]`. `-Recurse` goes into every subfolder, and `-Force` includes hidden items or overwrites existing ones.

Reading and writing text:

- `Get-Content file` returns an **array**, an ordered list of values, with one string per line; add `-Raw` to get the whole file as one string.
- `Set-Content` replaces a file's contents, `Add-Content` adds to the end, and `Out-File` writes what would appear on screen.
- Files store text as bytes, following an **encoding**: a rule for turning letters into numbers. PowerShell 7 uses **UTF-8** (without a byte-order mark); add `-Encoding` when another tool expects something else.

Build paths with `Join-Path` and `Split-Path` instead of gluing text together. Linux and macOS separate folders with `/` and Windows with `\`, and both cmdlets handle that for you.

Commands that delete or change things support `-WhatIf` (show what would happen) and `-Confirm` (ask first): run `Remove-Item -Recurse -WhatIf` before the real thing.

The same cmdlets also work on other data stores, called **providers**, which appear as drives: `Env:` (environment variables, the settings passed to every program), `Variable:`, `Function:`, `Alias:`, and on Windows `HKLM:` (Windows' settings database) and `Cert:` (security certificates). `Get-PSDrive` lists them, so `Get-ChildItem Env:` lists environment variables just like files.
concepts.code:
$dir = Join-Path ([IO.Path]::GetTempPath()) 'ps-demo'
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $dir -Force | Out-Null
Set-Location $dir
Set-Content -Path notes.txt -Value 'first line'
Add-Content -Path notes.txt -Value 'second line'
Get-Content notes.txt                 # first line / second line
(Get-Content notes.txt).Count         # 2   (an array of lines)
Copy-Item notes.txt backup.txt
Test-Path backup.txt                  # True
Get-ChildItem -Filter *.txt | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name   # backup.txt notes.txt
Remove-Item backup.txt -WhatIf        # What if: Performing the operation "Remove File" ...
Split-Path (Join-Path $dir 'notes.txt') -Leaf   # notes.txt
Get-ChildItem Env: | Select-Object -First 2 Name   # environment as a drive
takeaways: Get-ChildItem, Copy-Item, Remove-Item and friends work on any provider
Get-Content returns an array of lines; -Raw returns one string
Join-Path for paths, -WhatIf before anything destructive
pitfalls: Gluing paths together with '\' in scripts that must also run on Linux or macOS.

quiz.q: What does `Get-Content log.txt` return for a 3-line file?
quiz.explain: Get-Content emits one string per line; use -Raw to get a single string.

quiz.q: What is `-WhatIf` for?
options: Showing what a command would do without doing it
Running a command only if a condition is true
quiz.explain: -WhatIf describes the operation instead of performing it.

concepts.name: Operators, if, switch and loops
concepts.summary: Compare with -eq, -like and -match, make decisions with if and switch, and repeat work with foreach, for and while.
concepts.why: PowerShell's dash-style comparisons and its habit of ignoring capitals surprise everyone who has used another language.
concepts.body:
To compare values, PowerShell uses **operators** written as words with a dash: `-eq` (equal), `-ne` (not equal), `-gt` (greater than), `-ge` (greater or equal), `-lt` (less than) and `-le` (less or equal). The usual `>` and `<` are taken: `>` sends output into a file (**output redirection**).

For text, `-like` matches with wildcards, a simple **glob pattern** (`*` any characters, `?` one character). `-match` uses a **regular expression**, a mini-language for text patterns, and saves what matched in `$Matches`; `-replace` replaces text using one. For lists, `-contains` (list on the left) and `-in` (list on the right) check membership.

All of these ignore capitals by default. Add a `c` for case-sensitive versions: `-ceq`, `-cmatch`.

A surprise: with a list of values on the left, a comparison filters the list instead of answering True or False. `1, 5, 9 -gt 4` gives `5, 9`. That is why `$null -eq $x` puts `$null` first: if `$x` held a list, the answer would otherwise be a filtered list.

A **conditional** runs code only when a condition holds: `if (...) { } elseif (...) { } else { }`. `switch` compares one value against several cases and supports `-Wildcard`, `-Regex` and code conditions. Unlike most languages, **every** matching case runs unless you `break`, and given a list, `switch` handles each item in turn.

A **loop** repeats code, and each pass is one **iteration**:

- the `foreach ($item in $list) { }` statement: fast, for data already loaded;
- the `ForEach-Object { $_ }` cmdlet: handles pipeline input one item at a time as it arrives;
- `for ($i = 0; $i -lt 10; $i++) { }` counts (`$i++` adds 1), and `while` and `do { } while` repeat as long as a condition holds.

`1..5` is the range of numbers 1 to 5, and conditions combine with `-and`, `-or` and `-not` (or `!`).
concepts.code:
$n = 7
if ($n -gt 5) { 'big' } elseif ($n -gt 2) { 'medium' } else { 'small' }   # big
'Hello' -eq 'hello'               # True   (case-insensitive by default)
'Hello' -ceq 'hello'              # False
'report.csv' -like '*.csv'        # True
'v2.15' -match 'v(\d+)\.(\d+)'    # True
$Matches[1]                       # 2
'b' -in 'a', 'b', 'c'             # True
1, 5, 9 -gt 4                     # 5 / 9   (a collection on the left filters!)
switch -Wildcard ('error.log') {
  '*.log' { 'log file' }          # log file
  'err*'  { 'error-ish' }         # error-ish  (every matching case runs)
}
foreach ($i in 1..3) { "item $i" }      # item 1 / item 2 / item 3
$i = 0; while ($i -lt 3) { $i++ }; $i   # 3
takeaways: -eq -gt -like -match ignore capitals unless prefixed with c
A list on the left of a comparison gets filtered
switch runs every matching case; foreach statement vs ForEach-Object cmdlet
pitfalls: Writing `if ($x > 5)`: > is redirection and creates a file named 5.

quiz.q: What does `if ($count > 10) { ... }` actually do?
quiz.explain: In PowerShell > is output redirection; use -gt to compare.

quiz.q: What does `'a','b','a' -eq 'a'` return?
quiz.explain: With a list on the left, -eq returns the matching items.

concepts.name: Arrays and hashtables
concepts.summary: Create and use arrays, growable lists, hashtables (key/value lookup tables) and ordered hashtables.
concepts.why: Collections and key/value maps hold the data of every non-trivial script.
concepts.body:
**Arrays**, ordered lists of values, are created with commas or `@( )`: `$a = 1, 2, 3` or `$a = @('x', 'y')`. Positions, called **indexes**, count from 0, and negative ones count from the end: `$a[0]`, `$a[-1]`; slices with ranges: `$a[0..1]`. `$a.Count` gives the length. Arrays are **fixed-size**: `$a += 4` builds a whole new array each time, which is fine for a handful of items and slow for thousands. For growing collections use .NET's list type `[System.Collections.Generic.List[object]]` (or `List[string]` to hold only strings) and `.Add()`.

`@( ... )` around a command **guarantees an array**, even when the command returns zero or one item, so `.Count` and indexing always behave.

**Hashtables** map keys to values, like a phone book where each name leads to a number: `$h = @{ Name = 'Ada'; Role = 'admin' }`. Read with `$h.Name` or `$h['Name']`, add by assigning a new key, test with `.ContainsKey()`, remove with `.Remove()`. Keys are case-insensitive by default. A plain hashtable does not keep insertion order; `[ordered]@{ }` does, which matters for output and JSON.

To loop over a hashtable, iterate `$h.GetEnumerator()` (giving `.Key` and `.Value`) or `$h.Keys`. Hashtables are also used for **splatting**: `$params = @{ Path = '.'; Recurse = $true }; Get-ChildItem @params` passes each key as a parameter of that name, which keeps long commands readable.
concepts.code:
$fruits = @('apple', 'banana')
$fruits += 'cherry'                   # creates a NEW array
$fruits[0]; $fruits[-1]               # apple / cherry
$fruits.Count                         # 3
$fruits -contains 'kiwi'              # False
$list = [System.Collections.Generic.List[string]]::new()
$list.Add('fast'); $list.Count        # 1   (use for big, growing lists)
$user = @{ Name = 'Ada'; Role = 'admin' }
$user.Name                            # Ada
$user['role']                         # admin  (keys are case-insensitive)
$user.Email = 'ada@example.com'       # add a key
$user.ContainsKey('Email')            # True
$ordered = [ordered]@{ b = 2; a = 1 }
$ordered.Keys -join ','               # b,a   (insertion order kept)
foreach ($kv in $ordered.GetEnumerator()) { "$($kv.Key)=$($kv.Value)" }   # b=2 / a=1
$params = @{ Path = $PSHOME; Filter = '*.json' }
@(Get-ChildItem @params).Count -gt 0  # True   (splatting + @() for an array)
takeaways: Arrays: 1, 2, 3 or @(); += copies, use List[T] for growth
@{ } hashtable, [ordered]@{ } keeps key order
Splat a hashtable of parameters with @params
pitfalls: Building a large result with `$results += $item` in a loop: it is quadratic.

quiz.q: A command returns a single string 'abc'. What is `$r[0]` without @() and `@($r)[0]` with it?
quiz.explain: Indexing a lone string returns a character; @() wraps the result in an array so [0] is the whole item.

quiz.q: What does `Get-ChildItem @opts` do when $opts is a hashtable?
options: Passes each key/value as a named parameter
Passes the hashtable as one argument
quiz.explain: Splatting expands the hashtable's keys into parameter names and values.

concepts.name: Functions and parameters
concepts.summary: Write functions whose parameters have types, defaults, checks and on/off switches, and call them the PowerShell way.
concepts.why: Functions with proper parameters behave like real cmdlets: Tab completion, input checks and help for free.
concepts.body:
A **function** is a named, reusable piece of code. Define one with `function Verb-Noun { param(...) ... }`. Use an approved verb so it fits in with the built-in commands. The `param()` block declares parameters:

- a **type** like `[string]` or `[int]` converts and validates the input,
- a **default value**, used when the caller leaves it out: `[string]$Word = 'Hello'`,
- `[Parameter(Mandatory)]` asks for the value if it is missing (or fails when nobody is there to answer),
- **validation** attributes, checks written in square brackets that reject bad input: `[ValidateSet('a','b')]`, `[ValidateRange(1,10)]`, `[ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]`, `[ValidatePattern('^\d+$')]`,
- `[switch]$Force` is an on/off flag that is `$true` when present.

**Calling** works like any cmdlet: `Get-Greeting -Name Ada -Shout`, or positionally `Get-Greeting Ada`. Never call with parentheses and commas: `Add(2, 3)` passes a **single array** to the first parameter. Parentheses and commas are only for .NET methods.

What a function **returns** is everything it outputs: any value not assigned or discarded goes to the pipeline. `return $x` just outputs `$x` and exits. Discard unwanted output with `$null = ...` or `| Out-Null`.

Pressing Tab completes your parameter names, and a comment-based help block (`<# .SYNOPSIS ... #>`) makes `Get-Help` work for your function.
concepts.code:
function Get-Greeting {
  param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory)]
    [string]$Name,
    [ValidateSet('Hello', 'Hi', 'Welcome')]
    [string]$Word = 'Hello',
    [switch]$Shout
  )
  $text = "$Word, $Name!"
  if ($Shout) { $text = $text.ToUpper() }
  $text                              # output = return value
}
Get-Greeting -Name Ada               # Hello, Ada!
Get-Greeting Bob -Word Hi -Shout     # HI, BOB!
# Get-Greeting -Name Cy -Word Yo     # error: "Yo" does not belong to the set
function Add-Numbers($a, $b) { $a + $b }
Add-Numbers 2 3                      # 5      (spaces, no commas)
Add-Numbers(2, 3)                    # 2 / 3  ($a got the array 2,3; $b is empty)
takeaways: param() with types, defaults, Mandatory, Validate* and [switch]
Call functions like cmdlets: Name -Param value, no parentheses or commas
Every uncaptured value is output; return just exits
pitfalls: Calling `MyFunc($a, $b)` like a method, which passes one array argument.

quiz.q: How do you call a function `Add-Numbers($a, $b)` with 2 and 3?
quiz.explain: Arguments are space-separated; a comma makes an array.

quiz.q: What is the value of a [switch]$Force parameter when the caller omits -Force?
quiz.explain: A switch is false unless the flag is supplied.

concepts.name: Scripts, execution policy and profiles
concepts.summary: Write .ps1 scripts with a param block, run them on any system, and understand execution policy, dot-sourcing and your startup profile.
concepts.why: Saving work as scripts is how ad-hoc commands become repeatable automation.
concepts.body:
A script is a `.ps1` file. It can start with a `param()` block, exactly like a function, so it gets named parameters, input checks and Tab completion. Run it with its path, `./backup.ps1 -Source ./docs`, or from another shell with `pwsh -File ./backup.ps1`. On Linux and macOS, a first line of `#!/usr/bin/env pwsh` (a shebang, telling the system which program runs the file) plus `chmod +x` (mark the file as runnable) also works.

Useful automatic variables: `$PSScriptRoot` is the folder containing the script, the reliable starting point for paths to files next to it; `$PSCommandPath` is the script's full path. `#Requires -Version 7.0` or `#Requires -Modules Name` stop the script early if requirements are missing. `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` turns uses of variables and properties that don't exist into errors.

**Execution policy**, a setting that applies on Windows only, controls whether scripts may run (`Restricted`, `RemoteSigned`, `AllSigned`, `Unrestricted`, `Bypass`). Check it with `Get-ExecutionPolicy -List`; developers typically use `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`. Downloaded files are marked and may need `Unblock-File`. It is a safety feature against accidents, **not a security boundary**.

**Dot-sourcing** `. ./helpers.ps1` runs a script in the current **scope** (your current set of variables and functions), so its functions and variables remain available. Your **PowerShell profile**, a script at the path in `$PROFILE`, is dot-sourced at startup; put aliases, functions and prompt tweaks there.
concepts.code:
# file: backup.ps1
#Requires -Version 7.0
param(
  [Parameter(Mandatory)][string]$Source,
  [string]$Destination = (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'backups')
)
Set-StrictMode -Version Latest
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Destination -Force | Out-Null
$stamp = Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd-HHmmss'
Compress-Archive -Path $Source -DestinationPath "$Destination/backup-$stamp.zip"
"Saved to $Destination"
# Running it:
#   ./backup.ps1 -Source ./docs
#   pwsh -File ./backup.ps1 -Source ./docs      (from bash, cmd, cron...)
# Windows only:
#   Get-ExecutionPolicy -List
#   Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
# . ./helpers.ps1    # dot-source: load its functions into this scope
# $PROFILE           # path of your startup profile script
takeaways: A param() block at the top makes a script take named parameters
$PSScriptRoot anchors relative paths
Execution policy is a Windows safety setting, not security; dot-source to import
pitfalls: Using relative paths that depend on the caller's current directory instead of $PSScriptRoot.

quiz.q: A script reads './config.json' and fails when run from another folder. What is the fix?
quiz.explain: Relative paths resolve against the current location; $PSScriptRoot is the script's own folder.

quiz.q: What does dot-sourcing `. ./lib.ps1` do?
options: Runs lib.ps1 in a child scope
Runs it in the current scope so its definitions remain
quiz.explain: Dot-sourcing keeps the functions and variables lib.ps1 defines in the caller's scope.

concepts.name: Output, formatting and Write-Host
concepts.summary: Know the difference between output and display: Write-Output, Write-Host, Write-Verbose, Format-* and Out-*.
concepts.why: Mixing up output and display is the top reason PowerShell functions return garbage or print nothing.
concepts.body:
PowerShell separates **output** (objects sent down the pipeline, which callers can capture) from **display** (what the PowerShell window shows you). Anything not captured is output; `Write-Output` is the explicit form but rarely needed.

For messages, use the cmdlet for the purpose, because each writes to its own separate channel, a **stream**, not to the output:

- `Write-Verbose` (shown with `-Verbose`), `Write-Debug`, `Write-Warning`, `Write-Error`,
- `Write-Information` and `Write-Host` for user-facing text; `Write-Host` can add colour.

That way `$result = My-Function` captures only data, not chatter.

**Format-Table**, **Format-List** and **Format-Wide** turn objects into formatting instructions for display. Use them only at the **end** of a pipeline: after `Format-Table` you no longer have the original objects, so sorting, exporting or reading properties breaks. To get text, use `Out-String`; to write to a file, `Out-File` or `Set-Content`; to save data, prefer `Export-Csv` or `ConvertTo-Json`.

The `-f` format operator builds strings: `'{0} is {1:N1} GB' -f $name, $size`, with .NET format codes like `N2`, `P0` (percent) and `yyyy-MM-dd` for dates. `Out-Null` or `$null = ...` discard output you do not want.
concepts.code:
function Get-Info {
  [CmdletBinding()] param()
  Write-Verbose 'collecting'                  # only shown with -Verbose
  Write-Host 'progress...' -ForegroundColor Cyan   # display, not output
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'disk'; UsedGB = 41.53 }
}
$r = Get-Info                                 # screen shows: progress...
$r.UsedGB                                     # 41.53  (the object was captured)
Get-Info -Verbose | Out-Null                  # VERBOSE: collecting
Get-ChildItem $PSHOME -File | Select-Object -First 3 Name, Length |
  Format-Table -AutoSize                      # display only, at the very end
'{0} is {1:N1} GB' -f 'disk', 41.53           # disk is 41.5 GB
$text = Get-Process -Id $PID | Out-String     # render as one string
$text.GetType().Name                          # String
takeaways: Output goes down the pipeline; Write-Host only displays
Write-Verbose / Warning / Error keep messages out of captured data
Format-* only at the end; Out-String, Export-Csv or ConvertTo-Json for data
pitfalls: `Get-Process | Format-Table | Export-Csv`: the CSV contains formatting objects, not processes.

quiz.q: A function prints a message with Write-Output and returns a number. What does `$x = Func` contain?
quiz.explain: Write-Output sends to the output stream, so both values are captured; use Write-Verbose or Write-Host for messages.

quiz.q: Where should Format-Table appear in a pipeline?
quiz.explain: Format cmdlets produce display instructions; later commands cannot use the original objects.

concepts.name: Custom objects, JSON and CSV
concepts.summary: Create [pscustomobject] records and move data in and out of JSON, CSV and web APIs.
concepts.why: Real scripts read data from files and APIs, reshape it and write reports.
concepts.body:
`[pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'web1'; CPU = 72 }` creates an object with those properties, in that order. Custom objects flow through the pipeline like any cmdlet output: you can filter, sort, group and export them. They are the right way to return structured results from your functions, instead of formatted strings.

**JSON** is a common text format for structured data. `ConvertTo-Json` turns objects into JSON text (**serialization**) (mind `-Depth`: the default of 2 truncates deeper nesting, with a warning), and `ConvertFrom-Json` reads (**parses**) JSON text into objects; `-AsHashtable` gives hashtables instead. Read a file with `Get-Content file.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json`.

**CSV** is a table saved as text, one row per line with commas between the values. `Export-Csv` writes objects (PowerShell 7 no longer adds a type header, so `-NoTypeInformation` is optional), and `Import-Csv` reads rows back as objects whose property values are **all strings**. Cast before comparing numbers: `[int]$_.CPU -gt 50`.

**Web APIs**: `Invoke-RestMethod` calls a **web API**, a service that programs talk to over the web, and converts its JSON reply into objects automatically; `Invoke-WebRequest` gives the raw reply, including its status code (like 200 for OK or 404 for not found) and headers.

To add a property to an existing object use `Add-Member` or `Select-Object *, @{ Name = 'New'; Expression = { ... } }`. `ForEach-Object Name` (member name shorthand) pulls a single property out of each object.
concepts.code:
Set-Location ([IO.Path]::GetTempPath())
$servers = @(
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'web1'; CPU = 72; Env = 'prod' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'web2'; CPU = 15; Env = 'prod' }
  [pscustomobject]@{ Name = 'dev1'; CPU = 90; Env = 'dev' }
)
$servers | Where-Object CPU -gt 50 | ForEach-Object Name   # web1 / dev1
$json = $servers | ConvertTo-Json -Compress
$json.Substring(0, 38)              # [{"Name":"web1","CPU":72,"Env":"prod"}
$back = $json | ConvertFrom-Json
$back[2].CPU + 1                    # 91
$servers | Export-Csv servers.csv
(Import-Csv servers.csv)[0].CPU.GetType().Name     # String  (CSV is text)
@(Import-Csv servers.csv | Where-Object { [int]$_.CPU -gt 50 }).Count   # 2
$servers | Group-Object Env | ForEach-Object { "$($_.Name): $($_.Count)" }   # dev: 1 / prod: 2  (groups sorted by name)
# $repo = Invoke-RestMethod https://api.github.com/repos/PowerShell/PowerShell
# $repo.stargazers_count          # JSON response arrives as objects
takeaways: [pscustomobject]@{ } is the standard record type
ConvertTo-Json needs -Depth for nested data
Import-Csv values are strings; cast before numeric comparisons
pitfalls: Comparing Import-Csv values as numbers without casting: '9' -gt '50' is True as strings.

quiz.q: After Import-Csv, `$row.Count -gt 100` behaves oddly. Why?
options: CSV values are strings, so the comparison is textual
quiz.explain: Every imported value is a string; cast with [int] to compare numerically.

quiz.q: What can go wrong with `$deep | ConvertTo-Json` on nested data?
options: Levels beyond the default depth of 2 are truncated to strings
quiz.explain: Raise -Depth to serialize deeper structures fully.

concepts.name: Error handling: try/catch and -ErrorAction
concepts.summary: Terminating vs non-terminating errors, -ErrorAction Stop, try/catch/finally, $ErrorActionPreference and native exit codes.
concepts.why: Without understanding the two kinds of errors, try/catch silently fails to catch most cmdlet errors.
concepts.body:
Errors usually arrive as an **exception**, an error signal raised while code runs. Handling them well (**exception handling**) starts with knowing that PowerShell has two kinds of errors:

- **Non-terminating** errors, the default for most cmdlets: the error is reported (and added to `$Error`) but the command continues with the next item. `try/catch` does **not** see these.
- **Terminating** errors: `throw`, .NET exceptions, and any error raised with `-ErrorAction Stop`. These stop the current statement and can be caught.

So the standard pattern is `try { Some-Cmdlet -ErrorAction Stop } catch { ... }`. Inside `catch`, `$_` is the **ErrorRecord**: `$_.Exception.Message`, `$_.Exception.GetType()`, `$_.TargetObject`, `$_.InvocationInfo.ScriptLineNumber`. You can catch specific exception types first and a general `catch` last. `finally` always runs, for cleanup.

`-ErrorAction`, one of the **common parameters** every cmdlet accepts, sets the behaviour per call: `Stop`, `Continue` (default), `SilentlyContinue`, `Ignore`. `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` at the top of a script makes all cmdlet errors terminating, the PowerShell equivalent of `set -e` in the Bash shell. `-ErrorVariable errs` collects a call's errors into a variable.

**Ordinary programs** (git, docker) don't raise PowerShell errors; check `$LASTEXITCODE`, their **exit code** (0 means success, anything else a failure), after them, or in 7.4+ set `$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true` so a non-zero exit becomes an error. `$?` tells whether the last command succeeded.
takeaways: try/catch only sees terminating errors; add -ErrorAction Stop
$_ in catch is the ErrorRecord; finally always runs
Check $LASTEXITCODE after native programs
pitfalls: Wrapping a cmdlet in try/catch without -ErrorAction Stop and wondering why catch never runs.

quiz.q: `try { Remove-Item missing.txt } catch { 'oops' }` prints an error but not 'oops'. Why?
options: Remove-Item's error is non-terminating; add -ErrorAction Stop
quiz.explain: Most cmdlet errors are non-terminating and bypass catch unless made terminating.

quiz.q: How do you detect that `git push` failed in a script?
quiz.explain: Native programs report failure through their exit code, stored in $LASTEXITCODE.

concepts.name: Advanced functions and pipeline input
concepts.summary: Use [CmdletBinding()], begin/process/end blocks and ValueFromPipeline to write functions that act like real cmdlets.
concepts.why: Functions that accept pipeline input combine with built-in cmdlets and handle large inputs one item at a time.
concepts.body:
Adding `[CmdletBinding()]` above `param()` turns a function into an **advanced function**. It gains the common parameters (`-Verbose`, `-ErrorAction`, `-WhatIf` when declared...) and the `$PSCmdlet` object.

To accept **pipeline input**, mark a parameter with `ValueFromPipeline` (the whole object binds) or `ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName` (a property with the same name, or an `[Alias()]`, binds). The function body is then split into blocks:

- `begin { }` runs once before the first item: initialise counters, open connections,
- `process { }` runs **once per pipeline item**, with the parameter bound to that item,
- `end { }` runs once at the end: totals, cleanup.

Without a `process` block the whole body acts like `end` and only sees the last item. Declare array parameters (`[string[]]`) and loop inside `process`, so the function works both when piped and when called with several values directly.

For commands that change things, add `[CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess)]` and guard changes with `if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($target, 'Delete')) { ... }`. Your function then supports `-WhatIf` and `-Confirm` automatically, just like `Remove-Item`. Emit objects with `[pscustomobject]` rather than formatted text so callers can keep piping.
takeaways: [CmdletBinding()] adds common parameters like -Verbose
ValueFromPipeline / ByPropertyName bind piped objects
begin once, process per item, end once; SupportsShouldProcess adds -WhatIf
pitfalls: Omitting the process block, so a piped function only handles the last item.

quiz.q: A pipeline-aware function has no begin/process/end blocks. What does it see when 5 items are piped in?
options: All 5 items one at a time
quiz.explain: Without explicit blocks the body runs as end, after the pipeline, with the last bound value.

quiz.q: What does SupportsShouldProcess give your function?
quiz.explain: Combined with $PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess(), it makes -WhatIf and -Confirm work.

concepts.name: Modules and the PowerShell Gallery
concepts.summary: Install modules (packages of commands) from the PowerShell Gallery and package your own functions as a module with a manifest.
concepts.why: Modules are how PowerShell code is shared, versioned and reused across scripts and teams.
concepts.body:
A **module** is a package of commands. Most of PowerShell itself ships as modules, and thousands more (Az for Azure, Pester for testing, PSScriptAnalyzer for checking code for common mistakes, Microsoft.Graph) are published on the **PowerShell Gallery**.

In PowerShell 7.4+ the **PSResourceGet** cmdlets manage them: `Find-PSResource`, `Install-PSResource -Scope CurrentUser`, `Update-PSResource`. The older PowerShellGet commands (`Install-Module`) still work. Modules are found in the folders listed in `$env:PSModulePath` and **auto-loaded** the first time you use one of their commands, so `Import-Module` is mostly needed for modules outside those folders or to reload with `-Force` during development.

Your own **script module** is a `.psm1` file with functions; put it in a folder of the same name. Control what is public with `Export-ModuleMember` or, better, a **module manifest** (`.psd1`) created by `New-ModuleManifest`, which declares the version, author, dependencies and `FunctionsToExport`. Explicit exports keep helper functions private and make auto-loading fast.

Common layout: one function per `.ps1` file in `Public/` and `Private/` folders, dot-sourced by the `.psm1`, plus Pester tests. `Get-Command -Module Name` lists a module's commands and `Get-Module` shows what is loaded.
concepts.code:
Find-PSResource -Name Pester                        # search the PowerShell Gallery
Install-PSResource -Name Pester -Scope CurrentUser  # PSResourceGet (7.4+)
Get-Module -ListAvailable Pester | Select-Object Name, Version
# Your own module: MyTools/MyTools.psm1
#   function Get-Answer { Get-InternalValue }
#   function Get-InternalValue { 42 }               # helper, kept private
New-ModuleManifest ./MyTools/MyTools.psd1 -RootModule MyTools.psm1 `
  -ModuleVersion 1.0.0 -FunctionsToExport Get-Answer
Import-Module ./MyTools -Force
Get-Answer                                          # 42
Get-Command -Module MyTools | Select-Object -ExpandProperty Name   # Get-Answer
Get-InternalValue                                   # error: not recognized (private)
$env:PSModulePath -split [IO.Path]::PathSeparator   # where modules are discovered
takeaways: Install-PSResource gets modules from the PowerShell Gallery
Modules on $env:PSModulePath auto-load on first use
A .psd1 manifest declares version and exported functions
pitfalls: Exporting every function with wildcards, which exposes helpers and slows auto-loading.

quiz.q: Why is Import-Module often unnecessary?
options: Modules on PSModulePath auto-load when you first use a command
quiz.explain: Command discovery auto-imports modules found in PSModulePath.

quiz.q: What does FunctionsToExport in a module manifest control?
options: Which functions callers can see after import
quiz.explain: Only the listed functions are public; the rest stay internal to the module.

concepts.name: Jobs, parallelism and remoting
concepts.summary: Run work concurrently with Start-ThreadJob and ForEach-Object -Parallel, and on other machines with Invoke-Command.
concepts.why: Parallel and remote execution turn slow, one-machine-at-a-time scripts into fleet automation.
concepts.body:
PowerShell has several ways to run work at the same time (**concurrency**):

- **Start-Job** runs a script block in a separate background **process**, a whole new running program. Isolated but heavy (a new pwsh starts each time).
- **Start-ThreadJob** runs it on a **thread**, a second line of work inside the same program: much lighter, the usual choice. Both return job objects; collect results with `Receive-Job` (`-Wait` to block) and clean up with `Remove-Job`.
- **ForEach-Object -Parallel** (PowerShell 7) processes pipeline items at the same time, each in a **runspace** (an isolated place to run code), with `-ThrottleLimit` (default 5) capping concurrency.

Code in a job or a parallel block cannot see your variables. Pass values with the **`$using:`** scope modifier, which copies them in: `$using:token`. Do not modify shared collections from parallel blocks; output results and collect them instead.

Running things in parallel pays off for **I/O-bound** work, which mostly waits on the network or disk, like web calls, remote commands and file copies. For tiny CPU tasks, the overhead of runspaces can make it slower than a plain loop.

**Remoting** runs commands on other machines: `Invoke-Command -ComputerName srv1, srv2 -ScriptBlock { ... }` executes in parallel on all of them over **WinRM** (Windows' remote-management service), and `-HostName` uses **SSH**, the standard secure remote-login method, which works on every system. `Enter-PSSession` lets you type commands on the remote computer; `New-PSSession` keeps a reusable connection. Results come back as copies rebuilt from text: properties only, no methods.
takeaways: Start-ThreadJob is light, Start-Job isolates in a process
ForEach-Object -Parallel with -ThrottleLimit for concurrent pipelines
$using:var passes local values into jobs, parallel blocks and remote sessions
pitfalls: Referencing $myVar inside -Parallel or a job without $using: and getting $null.

quiz.q: Inside ForEach-Object -Parallel, how do you read the caller's $limit variable?
quiz.explain: Each parallel runspace is isolated; $using: copies the caller's value in.

quiz.q: Which is the lightest way to run a background task in PowerShell 7?
quiz.explain: Thread jobs run in the same process, avoiding the cost of starting a new pwsh.

concepts.name: Using .NET and PowerShell classes
concepts.summary: Call any .NET API with [Type]::Method(), create objects with ::new(), define PowerShell classes and compile C# with Add-Type.
concepts.why: When no cmdlet exists, the entire .NET library is one line away, and classes give you real types.
concepts.body:
PowerShell runs on .NET, so every .NET type is available. **Static members**, which belong to a type itself rather than to one object, use `[Type]::Member`: `[math]::Round(2.567, 2)`, `[System.IO.Path]::GetExtension($f)`, `[datetime]::Parse('2026-01-15')`, `[guid]::NewGuid()`. Common **namespaces** (the dotted prefixes that group types, like `System.IO`) may be shortened (`[IO.Path]`), and a `using namespace System.Text` line at the top of a script lets you write `[StringBuilder]`. Create instances with `[Type]::new(args)` (or the older `New-Object`).

**PowerShell classes** (since 5.0), blueprints for your own kinds of object, define real .NET types with typed properties, **constructors** (set-up code that runs when an object is created), methods, static members, **inheritance** (one class building on another) and **enums** (fixed sets of named values):

- methods must declare a return type and use `return` explicitly; unlike functions, stray values are **not** output,
- reference the instance with `$this`,
- override `ToString()` to control how objects appear in strings.

Classes are useful for data with built-in checks and for advanced features like custom validation attributes and DSC resources (Desired State Configuration, PowerShell's system-configuration feature). Limitations: a class must be defined before the code that uses it is read, and changing a class inside a module needs a fresh PowerShell session.

`Add-Type -TypeDefinition` compiles C# source on the fly, for speed-critical code or to call functions in the operating system's own libraries (P/Invoke). Compiled types cannot be unloaded from the session, so rename them while iterating.
concepts.code:
[System.IO.Path]::GetExtension('report.final.csv')   # .csv
[math]::Sqrt(144)                                    # 12
[datetime]::Parse('2026-01-15').DayOfWeek            # Thursday
$sb = [System.Text.StringBuilder]::new()
[void]$sb.Append('fast ').Append('strings')
$sb.ToString()                                       # fast strings
class Server {
  [string]$Name
  [int]$Cpu
  Server([string]$name, [int]$cpu) { $this.Name = $name; $this.Cpu = $cpu }
  [bool] IsBusy() { return $this.Cpu -gt 80 }
  [string] ToString() { return "$($this.Name) ($($this.Cpu)%)" }
}
$s = [Server]::new('web1', 92)
$s.IsBusy()                                          # True
"$s"                                                 # web1 (92%)
Add-Type -TypeDefinition 'public static class Calc { public static int Twice(int x) { return x * 2; } }'
[Calc]::Twice(21)                                    # 42
takeaways: [Type]::StaticMember and [Type]::new() reach all of .NET
Class methods need return types and explicit return
Add-Type compiles C# for speed or native interop
pitfalls: Expecting a class method to output values like a function: only the return value comes back.

quiz.q: How do you create a new System.Text.StringBuilder in modern PowerShell?
quiz.explain: ::new() calls the type's constructor; New-Object also works but is slower.

quiz.q: A class method contains `'debug'; return 5`. What does calling it return?
quiz.explain: In class methods only the return statement produces a value; other expressions are discarded.

concepts.name: Output semantics, unrolling and streams
concepts.summary: Why functions return extra values, how collections unroll in the pipeline, and how to send the six output streams elsewhere.
concepts.why: These rules explain the strangest PowerShell bugs: arrays that turn into single values, and results with unexpected extra items.
concepts.body:
**Everything uncaptured is output.** `return $x` is just "output $x and leave"; any earlier expression that produced a value, such as a .NET method returning an index (`ArrayList.Add`) or a cmdlet you forgot to silence, is output too, so the caller receives an array. Discard with `$null = ...`, `[void](...)` or `| Out-Null` (the first two are fastest).

**Unrolling**: when a collection is written to the pipeline, it is enumerated item by item. A function returning a one-element array therefore gives the caller a **scalar**, and an empty array gives nothing (`$null`). To return the collection itself, prefix it with the unary comma: `return , $list`. On the caller side, `@(...)` reliably turns any result into an array.

PowerShell has **six streams**: 1 Success (output), 2 Error, 3 Warning, 4 Verbose, 5 Debug, 6 Information. `Write-Host` writes to the Information stream since 5.0, which is why it can now be captured. Redirect by number: `2>&1` merges errors into output, `3> warnings.txt` saves warnings, `*> $null` silences everything, `*>&1` merges all streams into output.

`$null` comparisons also involve this: an empty pipeline result is a special "AutomationNull" that behaves as `$null` but, unlike `$null`, produces no iteration in `foreach`.
concepts.code:
function Get-Two { 'noise'; return 'value' }        # BOTH are output
(Get-Two).Count                                     # 2
function Get-One { return @(42) }
(Get-One).GetType().Name                            # Int32   (unrolled to a scalar)
function Get-Wrapped { return , @(42) }             # unary comma keeps the array
(Get-Wrapped).GetType().Name                        # Object[]
@(Get-One).Count                                    # 1       (@() forces an array)
function Get-None { return @() }
$null -eq (Get-None)                                # True
$al = [System.Collections.ArrayList]::new()
function Add-Item { $al.Add('x'); 'done' }          # Add returns an index...
Add-Item                                            # 0 / done  (leaked output)
$null = $al.Add('y')                                # discard it like this
function Get-Info { Write-Warning 'careful'; Write-Information 'fyi'; 'data' }
$out = Get-Info 3>&1 6>&1                           # merge warning + information
$out.Count                                          # 3
Get-Info *> $null                                   # silence every stream
takeaways: Every uncaptured value is output; return only exits
Collections unroll: return , $arr to keep one, @() to force an array
Streams 1-6; redirect with 2>&1, 3>, *> $null
pitfalls: Calling methods like ArrayList.Add() in a function without discarding the result, so the caller gets extra numbers.

quiz.q: A function ends with `return @('only')`. What type does the caller get?
quiz.explain: The one-element array is unrolled in the pipeline, leaving the single string.

quiz.q: Which redirection silences all streams of a command?
quiz.explain: *> redirects every stream; > and | Out-Null affect only the success stream.

concepts.name: Scopes, dot-sourcing and performance
concepts.summary: How variable scopes work, what $script: and $global: change, and the patterns that make PowerShell code fast.
concepts.why: Scope surprises cause silent bugs, and a few habits make scripts orders of magnitude faster on large data.
concepts.body:
Each script, function and script block runs in its own **scope**: its own set of variables. A child scope can **read** variables from its parents, but assigning creates a new **local variable** that hides the parent's one.

To change an outer variable, use a scope modifier: `$script:count` (the script's top level) or `$global:count` (everything until you close PowerShell). `$private:x` hides a variable from child scopes. Modules have their own isolated session state, so their internals do not leak into yours. Dot-sourcing runs a script in the caller's scope instead of a new one.

Usually it is better to **return** values than to modify outer variables; scope modifiers are best kept for module-level state.

Performance habits that matter on large inputs:

- Do not grow arrays with `+=`: assign the output of the loop (`$r = foreach (...) { ... }`) or use `List[T]`.
- The `foreach` **statement** and the `.Where()` / `.ForEach()` methods are much faster than `ForEach-Object` and `Where-Object` for data already loaded; the cmdlets shine when items arrive one by one.
- Filter left with cmdlet parameters, and discard output with `$null =` rather than `| Out-Null` in loops that run many times.
- Build strings with `-join` or a StringBuilder, not repeated `+=`.

Always measure with `Measure-Command { ... }` before and after an optimisation.
takeaways: Assignment creates a local variable; use $script: or $global: deliberately
Capture loop output instead of +=; prefer foreach and .Where() in memory
Measure-Command before and after optimising
pitfalls: Expecting a function's `$total += 1` to update the script's $total.

quiz.q: A script sets $n = 1; a function runs `$n = 5`. What is $n at script level afterwards?
quiz.explain: Assignment in the function creates a local $n; the script's variable is untouched.

quiz.q: Which builds a 100,000-item result fastest?
quiz.explain: Assigning the loop's output collects items once; += copies the whole array on every iteration.
